title: Diamond Caverns' Decorated Limestone
summary: Discovered July 14, 1859, near Park City and opened as a show cave within a month, Diamond Caverns cuts Mississippian Ste. Genevieve limestone in the same karst country as…
bodyMarkdown:
On July 14, 1859, an enslaved man held by landowner Jessie Coats found Diamond Caverns in a Kentucky valley near the road to [Mammoth Cave](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park), in what is now Park City. His name is not recorded in the [Diamond Caverns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_Caverns) history, a common gap for enslaved people whose discoveries made money for others. The first visitor thought the glittering calcite looked like diamonds, and the name stuck.

A survey crew went in the next day. After a month of labor to make the passages passable, the first tour group, the Kennedy Bridal Party, came through on August 19, 1859. Apart from short closures during the Civil War, the cave has drawn paying visitors ever since.

The cave sits in the same karst country as Mammoth Cave, whose own past runs from [saltpeter mining](/stories/mammoth-cave-saltpeter/) to tourism.

## Rock and water

The cave lies mostly in limestone laid down in the late Mississippian Period, when a shallow, warm sea covered most of Kentucky. Water dissolves the limestone and then gives the mineral back. Groundwater entering the cave carries nearly 250 times as much carbon dioxide as the cave air, so the gas escapes and calcite comes out of solution as travertine.

That slow chemistry built the formations visitors see: soda straws, stalactites, columns, flowstone, thin "bacon strip" draperies and cave pearls. The cave also shelters living things, including crickets, beetles, spiders, salamanders and crayfish.

Mammoth Cave holds up differently. There the limestones are capped by the [Big Clifty Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Clifty_Sandstone), a resistant layer that shields them from surface erosion. Sources for Diamond Caverns do not say whether that caprock covers its passages, so the comparison is best left to Mammoth itself.

## Owners and stewards

Five caver couples bought the property on July 7, 1999, and still own it: Gary and Susan Berdeaux, Larry and Mayo McCarty, Roger and Carol McClure, Stanley and Kay Sides, and Gordon and Judy Smith.

## Kentucky today

Diamond Caverns is open year-round. The cave stays at 58 degrees, and the tour runs about half a mile. Next door, [Mammoth Cave National Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park) was established on July 1, 1941, and protects the longest known cave system on Earth, with 426 surveyed miles of passages as of 2025. Together the two caves show how Kentucky's karst country became a place of science, labor and tourism, built on the work of people whose names were often left out.
